questions.q: Why does this lesson treat a third-party LLM prompt as data leaving your control?
options: Sending a prompt to a hosted model puts that data outside your organization's control the moment it's sent
LLM prompts are automatically deleted after every request
Third-party LLMs never store or process any input data
Prompts sent to hosted models stay entirely on the user's own machine
questions.explain: For practical purposes, anything pasted into a hosted model's prompt should be treated as having left your control.

questions.q: What should never be pasted into a third-party LLM prompt, per this lesson?
options: Real customer PII, API keys, connection strings, passwords, and unredacted production data
Synthetic or masked sample data
A schema with column names but no rows
A generic transformation spec with no real values
questions.explain: These are exactly the categories covered by Fabric & Real-Time Analytics's PII handling and secrets management lessons.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a confident-sounding LLM claim is not the same as a correct one?
options: Confident phrasing is a property of how language models generate text, not a signal of accuracy
LLMs are only confident when they are correct
Confidence and correctness always match in practice
Only human-written claims can ever be confident-sounding
questions.explain: What matters is whether a claim traces to something real and checkable, not how fluently it reads.

questions.q: Between an unverified confident claim and a claim tied to a specific log line and confirmed data, which does this lesson value more?
options: The claim tied to a specific log line and confirmed data
Whichever claim sounds more fluent
Neither — both are equally worthless
The unverified confident claim, because it's faster to produce
questions.explain: A checkable citation is worth more than any amount of fluent-sounding certainty.

questions.q: Does handing a task to an LLM transfer responsibility for the output away from the engineer?
options: No — the engineer who ships the draft is accountable for it, whether they typed it or reviewed an AI's draft
Yes — the AI vendor becomes fully responsible
Yes — responsibility disappears entirely once an LLM is involved
Only if the engineer explicitly disclaims the AI's involvement
questions.explain: "The AI suggested it" is never a valid explanation for a bad outcome that shipped to production.
